blocks.p: About this time, too, a great sickness broke out in the town of Mansoul, and most of the inhabitants were badly afflicted. Even the captains and men of war were brought low, and stayed weak for a long time together; so that if an invasion had come, neither the townsmen nor the field officers could have done anything to the purpose. Oh, how many pale faces, weak hands, feeble knees, and staggering men were now to be seen walking the streets of Mansoul! Here were groans, there gasps, and over there lay those who were ready to faint.

The garments Emmanuel had given them were in a sorry state as well. Some were ripped, some were torn, and all were filthy; and some hung so loosely on them that the next bush they passed was ready to pluck them off.

After some time spent in this sad and desolate condition, the town’s own preacher called for a day of fasting, so that the people might humble themselves for having been so wicked against the great Shaddai and his Son. He asked Captain Boanerges to preach, and when the day came, the captain’s text was this: “Cut it down; why should it use up the ground?” [Luke 13:7] And he made a very sharp sermon on it. First he showed what gave rise to the words, namely, that the fig tree was barren. Then he showed what the sentence contained, namely, repentance or utter ruin. Next he showed by whose authority the sentence was pronounced, and that was Shaddai’s own. And last of all he gave the reasons for the point, and so concluded. But he was so pointed in the application that he made poor Mansoul tremble. For this sermon, like the one before it, worked powerfully on the hearts of the men of Mansoul; it did much to keep awake those whom the earlier preaching had roused. So now, through the whole town, there was little or nothing to be seen or heard but sorrow, mourning, and woe.

After the sermon they gathered to consult on what was best to be done. “But,” said the town’s own preacher, “I will do nothing on my own judgment without taking advice from my neighbor Mr. Godly-Fear. If he understood our Prince’s mind better than we did before, he may well understand it now, as we turn back to what is right.”

So they sent for Mr. Godly-Fear, who came at once; and when they asked his further opinion on what they had best do, the old gentleman said: “It is my opinion that this town of Mansoul, in this day of her distress, should draw up a humble petition and send it to her offended Prince Emmanuel, asking that in his favor and grace he will turn to you again, and not keep his anger forever.”

The townsmen agreed to his advice as one and drew up their request at once. The next question was, Who would carry it? At last they all agreed to send it by the Lord Mayor. He accepted the task, set out on his journey, and came to the court of Shaddai, where Emmanuel the Prince of Mansoul had gone. But the gate was shut, and a strict watch was kept at it, so that the petitioner was forced to stand outside for a long time together. Then he asked that someone go in and tell the Prince who was standing at the gate, and on what business. So someone went and told Shaddai, and Emmanuel his Son, that the Lord Mayor of Mansoul stood outside the gate of the King’s court, asking to be admitted into the presence of the Prince, the King’s Son, and told them both what his errand was. But the Prince would not come down, nor allow the gate to be opened to him, but sent him an answer to this effect: “They have turned their back to me, and not their face; but now, in the time of their trouble, they say to me, ‘Arise, and save us.’ [Jer. 2:27] Can they not go now to Mr. Carnal-Security, to whom they went when they turned from me, and make him their leader, their lord, and their protection in their trouble? Why do they visit me now that they are in trouble, when in their prosperity they went astray?”

This answer made the Lord Mayor’s face go dark. It troubled him, it bewildered him, it tore at him sorely. And now he began to see once more what it meant to be friendly with Diabolonians such as Mr. Carnal-Security. When he saw that there was little help to be had at court for now, for himself or for his friends in Mansoul, he beat his breast and went home weeping, lamenting the pitiful state of Mansoul all the way.

When he came within sight of the town, the elders and chief men of Mansoul went out at the gate to meet him, greet him, and learn how he had fared at court. But he told his tale so mournfully that they all cried out, and grieved, and wept. They threw ashes and dust on their heads, put sackcloth around their waists, and went crying out through the town of Mansoul; and when the rest of the townsfolk saw it, they all mourned and wept too. So this was a day of rebuke and trouble and anguish for the town of Mansoul, and of great distress.

After a time, when they had composed themselves a little, they came together to consult again on what was still to be done. As before, they asked the advice of the reverend Mr. Godly-Fear. He told them there was no better way than to keep doing what they had done, and he did not want them to be discouraged at all by what they had met with at court, even if several of their petitions should be answered with nothing but silence or rebuke. “For,” he said, “it is the way of the wise Shaddai to make men wait and to exercise their patience; and it should be the way of those in need to be willing to wait for his time.”

Then they took courage and sent again, and again, and again, and again. There was not one day now, nor one hour that passed over Mansoul’s head, in which a man might not have met some rider or other on the road, sounding his horn as he galloped from Mansoul to the court of King Shaddai, every one of them carrying letters of petition on the town’s behalf, pleading for the Prince’s return. The road, I say, was full of messengers now, going and coming and passing one another, some from the court and some from Mansoul. And this was the work of the miserable town of Mansoul all that long, sharp, cold, and weary winter.

Now if you have not forgotten, you may remember my telling you before that, after Emmanuel had taken Mansoul and remodeled the town, many of the old Diabolonians still remained in various lurking places within its bounds. Some had come with the tyrant when he invaded and took the town; others had been born, bred, and raised there through unlawful unions. Their holes, dens, and hiding places were in, under, or around the town wall. Some of their names were the Lord Fornication, the Lord Adultery, the Lord Murder, the Lord Anger, the Lord Lasciviousness, the Lord Deceit, the Lord Evil-eye, the Lord Blasphemy, and that horrible villain, the old and dangerous Lord Covetousness. These, as I told you, with many more, still lived in Mansoul, even after Emmanuel had driven their prince Diabolus out of the castle.

Against these the good Prince had granted a commission to the Lord Willbewill and others, indeed to the whole town of Mansoul, to seek, take, secure, and destroy any or all of them they could lay hands on, because they were Diabolonians by nature, enemies of the Prince, and men who wanted to ruin the blessed town of Mansoul. But the town of Mansoul did not pursue this warrant. It neglected to hunt these Diabolonians down, to arrest, secure, and destroy them. So what did these villains do but take courage little by little, put out their heads, and show themselves to the people of the town? And, as I was told, some of the men of Mansoul grew too friendly with some of them, to the sorrow of the town, as you will hear more about in its proper time and place.

Well, when the Diabolonian lords who were left saw that Mansoul had offended Emmanuel her Prince by her sin, and that he had withdrawn and was gone, what did they do but plot the town’s ruin? So once upon a time they met at the hideout of one Mr. Mischief, another Diabolonian, and there they discussed how they might deliver Mansoul into the hands of Diabolus again. Some advised one way and some another, each according to his own liking. At last my Lord Lasciviousness proposed that it might be best, to begin with, for some of the Diabolonians in Mansoul to venture to offer themselves as servants to some of the natives of the town. “For,” he said, “if they do, and Mansoul takes them on, they may make the taking of the town much easier for us, and for Diabolus our lord, than it would otherwise be.”

But then the Lord Murder stood up and said, “This cannot be done just now. Mansoul is in a kind of rage at present, because our friend Mr. Carnal-Security has already ensnared her once and made her offend against her Prince; and how will she make peace with her lord again, except by offering up our heads? Besides, we know they have a commission to take us and kill us wherever they find us. So let us be as wise as foxes. When we are dead, we can do them no harm; but while we live, we can.”

So when they had tossed the matter back and forth, they agreed together that a letter should be sent off to Diabolus at once in their name, showing him the state of Mansoul, and how far it had fallen under its Prince’s frown. “We may also,” said some, “let him know what we intend, and ask his advice in the case.”
So a letter was drawn up at once, and these were its contents:
To our great lord, the Prince Diabolus, dwelling below in the infernal cave:

O great father and mighty Prince Diabolus, we, the true Diabolonians still remaining in the rebellious town of Mansoul, who received our being from you and our nourishment at your hands, cannot quietly or contentedly bear to see, as we do this day, how you are spoken against, disgraced, and reproached among the people of this town. Nor is your long absence any pleasure to us, since it is greatly to our harm.

The reason we write to our lord is that we are not altogether without hope that this town may become your home again. It has fallen far away from its Prince Emmanuel, and he has risen up and left them; and though they send, and send, and send, and send after him to come back to them, they cannot win him over, or get a good word from him.

There has also been of late, and still is, a very great sickness and faintness among them, not only among the poorer sort of the town, but among the lords, captains, and chief gentry of the place. (Only we who are Diabolonians by nature remain well, lively, and strong.) So between their great offense on the one hand and their dangerous sickness on the other, we judge that they lie open to your hand and power. If, therefore, it suits your horrible cunning, and the cunning of the other princes with you, to come and make an attempt to take Mansoul again, send us word, and we will be ready, to the utmost of our power, to deliver it into your hand. Or if what we have said does not seem best and most fitting to your fatherhood, send us your mind in a few words, and we are all ready to follow your counsel, at the risk of our lives and of whatever else we have.
Given under our hands on the day and date written above, after a private consultation at the house of Mr. Mischief, who is still alive and keeps his place in our desirable town of Mansoul.

When Mr. Profane (for he was the carrier) came with his letter to Hell-Gate Hill, he knocked at the brass gates to be let in. Then Cerberus the porter, for he is the keeper of that gate, opened to Mr. Profane, who handed him the letter he had brought from the Diabolonians in Mansoul. So Cerberus carried it in and presented it to Diabolus his lord, saying, “News, my lord, from Mansoul, from our trusty friends in Mansoul.”

Then Beelzebub, Lucifer, Apollyon, and the rest of the rabble there came together from every corner of the den to hear what news there was from Mansoul. So the letter was opened and read aloud, with Cerberus standing by; and when its contents had spread into every corner of the den, an order was given that the dead-man’s bell, the bell tolled for the dying, should be rung at once for joy. So the bell was rung, and the princes rejoiced that Mansoul was likely to come to ruin. And the clapper of the bell went, “The town of Mansoul is coming to live with us; make room for the town of Mansoul.” They rang this bell, then, because they hoped to have Mansoul again.

When they had performed this horrible ceremony of theirs, they gathered again to consult on what answer to send to their friends in Mansoul. Some advised one thing and some another; but at length, because the business required haste, they left the whole matter to the prince Diabolus, judging him the most proper lord of the place. So he drew up a letter as he thought fit, in answer to what Mr. Profane had brought, and sent it to the Diabolonians living in Mansoul by the same hand that had brought theirs to him. These were its contents:

To our offspring, the high and mighty Diabolonians who still live in the town of Mansoul: Diabolus, the great prince of Mansoul, wishes a prosperous outcome and conclusion to the many brave enterprises, conspiracies, and designs that, out of your love and respect for our honor, you have it in your hearts to attempt against Mansoul.

Beloved children and disciples, my Lord Fornication, Adultery, and the rest: here in our desolate den we have received, to our highest joy and satisfaction, your welcome letter by the hand of our trusty Mr. Profane. And to show how welcome your news was, we rang out our bell for gladness; for we rejoiced as much as we could when we saw that we still had friends in Mansoul, friends who seek our honor and our revenge in the ruin of that town. We rejoiced, too, to hear that they have sunk into a degenerate condition, that they have offended their Prince, and that he is gone. Their sickness pleases us as well, as do your health, might, and strength. We would be glad indeed, most horribly beloved, if we could get this town into our clutches again. Nor will we spare our wit, our cunning, our craft, or our hellish inventions to bring this brave beginning of yours to the conclusion we desire.

And take this for your comfort, our offspring and our brood: if we can surprise the town again and take it, we will try to put all your enemies to the sword, and will make you the great lords and captains of the place. Nor need you fear that, once we have it again, we will ever be thrown out afterward; for we will come with more strength, and take a far firmer hold than we did at first. Besides, it is the law of that Prince whom they now acknowledge that if we get them a second time, they will be ours forever.

You, therefore, our trusty Diabolonians, pry further still, and try to spy out the weaknesses of the town of Mansoul. We would also have you try to weaken them more and more yourselves. Send us word, too, of the means by which you think we had best attempt to win it back: whether by persuading them to a vain and loose life; or by tempting them to doubt and despair; or by blowing up the town with the gunpowder of pride and self-conceit. And you, brave Diabolonians, true sons of the pit, be always ready to make a most hideous assault from within when we are ready to storm the town from without. Now speed you in your project, as we speed in our desires, to the utmost power of our gates. This is the wish of your great Diabolus, Mansoul’s enemy, who trembles whenever he thinks of the judgment to come. All the blessings of the pit be on you; and so we close our letter.
Given at the mouth of the pit, by the joint consent of all the princes of darkness, to be sent to the force and power we still have remaining in Mansoul, by the hand of Mr. Profane.
By me, Diabolus.

This letter, as I said, was sent from the dark dungeon of Diabolus, by the hand of Mr. Profane, to the Diabolonians still lurking in Mansoul’s wall. When Mr. Profane returned to Mansoul, he went as usual to the house of Mr. Mischief, for that was where the conclave met and the plotters gathered. When they saw that their messenger had come back safe and sound, they were very glad. Then he gave them the letter from Diabolus; and when they had read and considered it, their gladness grew all the more. They asked him how their friends were: how their Lord Diabolus was, and Lucifer, and Beelzebub, and the rest of the den.

“Well, well, my lords,” answered Profane. “They are well, as well as anyone can be in that place. They also rang for joy at the reading of your letter,” he said, “as you saw for yourselves when you read theirs.”

Encouraged in their work by the letter, they went back to their scheming: how they might complete their Diabolonian design on Mansoul. The first thing they agreed on was to keep everything as secret from Mansoul as they could. “Don’t let it be known; don’t let Mansoul get wind of what we are planning against it.” The next thing was how, and by what means, they should try to bring about the ruin and overthrow of Mansoul; and one said this and another said that.

Then Mr. Deceit stood up and said, “My true Diabolonian friends, our lords, the high ones of the deep dungeon, put these three ways before us: first, whether we had best seek its ruin by making Mansoul loose and vain; second, or by driving them to doubt and despair; third, or by trying to blow them up with the gunpowder of pride and self-conceit.

“Now I think that if we tempt them to pride, that may do something; and if we tempt them to wantonness, that may help. But to my mind, if we could drive them to despair, that would hit the nail on the head. For then, first of all, we would have them questioning whether the love in their Prince’s heart toward them is real, and that will disgust him greatly. If this works well, it will soon make them give up their habit of sending petitions to him. Then farewell to earnest pleading for help and supplies; for this conclusion will lie naturally before them: ‘We may as well do nothing as do it to no purpose.’”
So they all agreed with Mr. Deceit as one man.

The next question was, “But how shall we bring this to pass?” And the same gentleman answered with what he thought the best way. “Let as many of our friends as are willing to risk themselves to advance their prince’s cause,” he said, “disguise themselves in other clothes, change their names, and go into the market like men from a far country, and offer to hire themselves out as servants to the famous town of Mansoul. Let them pretend to serve their masters as profitably as can be. For by doing this, if Mansoul hires them, they may in a short time so corrupt and defile the town that her present Prince will not only be offended with them further, but in the end will spit them out of his mouth. And when that is done, our prince Diabolus will prey on them with ease; yes, of themselves they will fall into the mouth of the eater.”

No sooner was this project proposed than it was warmly accepted, and every Diabolonian was eager to take part in so delicate an enterprise. But it was not thought fit that all should do it; so they picked out two or three, namely the Lord Covetousness, the Lord Lasciviousness, and the Lord Anger. The Lord Covetousness called himself by the name of Prudent-thrifty; the Lord Lasciviousness called himself Harmless-mirth; and the Lord Anger called himself Good-zeal.

So on a market day they came into the marketplace, three strapping fellows to look at, dressed in sheep’s russet, a plain homespun wool, which by now looked almost as white as the white robes of the men of Mansoul. And these men could speak the language of Mansoul well. So when they offered to hire themselves out to the townsmen, they were taken on at once; for they asked little in wages and promised to do their masters great service.

Mr. Mind hired Prudent-thrifty, and Mr. Godly-Fear hired Good-zeal. It is true that this fellow Harmless-mirth hung on hand a little, and could not find himself a master as quickly as the others did, because the town of Mansoul was keeping Lent just then, its season of fasting. But after a while, since Lent was nearly over, the Lord Willbewill hired Harmless-mirth to be both his attendant and his footman. And so they all found themselves masters.

Once these villains had got this far into the houses of the men of Mansoul, they quickly began to do great harm there. Being filthy, crafty, and sly, they soon corrupted the households they were in; they tainted their masters badly, especially this Prudent-thrifty and the one they called Harmless-mirth. It is true that the one who went under the mask of Good-zeal was not so well liked by his master, for the old man soon found that he was nothing but a counterfeit rascal. When the fellow saw this, he made a quick escape from the house; otherwise, I have no doubt, his master would have hanged him.

Well, when these vagabonds had carried their design this far and corrupted the town as much as they could, they next considered when their prince Diabolus from outside, and they from inside, should make their attempt to seize Mansoul. They all agreed that a market day would be best for that work. Why? Because then the townsfolk would be busy about their affairs; and always take this as a rule: when people are busiest with the world, they least fear a surprise. “Then, too,” they said, “we will be able to gather ourselves together for the work of our friends and lords with less suspicion. And on such a day, if we attempt our work and fail, then when they put us to flight we can more easily hide ourselves in the crowd and escape.”
